<a id="add-curtain-grid-lines"></a>

### Add curtain grid lines

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** add grid lines to this one curtain wall - vertical or horizontal, at these positions or into equal panels, with mullions if asked.

ADDS curtain grid lines to ONE curtain wall - the one picked in Revit - each new line running the full height of the wall (vertical) or its full length (horizontal, a transom), at the positions given or dividing the wall into equal panels, and puts mullions of a named type on each new line when one is named. Revit's Curtain Grid tool, typed: "divide this curtain wall into six panels", "add a transom at 1100". **THIS WALL ONLY.** The lines go on the wall's own curtain grid, and nothing on its family type is written, so no other wall changes with it - the answer gives the number of other walls on its type and says they are untouched. SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID is the one that changes a type's layout and spacing, for all its walls at once. Works on a wall that already has grid lines from its type: the new lines are additions beside them. ASSUMPTION for the proof: what a later change to the type's own grid does to lines added here - kept, moved or dropped - has not been measured. **ONE CURTAIN WALL AT A TIME.** Exactly one among what is handed in. Anything else handed in that is not a curtain wall is named in `notCurtain` and left alone; two curtain walls are refused, so each position lands on the wall it was meant for. A basic or stacked wall alone is refused by name. A curved wall is refused: along a curve, a position from the start is not one straight distance. **DIRECTION AND POSITIONS.** `direction` is vertical - lines running up the wall, each position a distance ALONG it from its START, the end it was drawn from - or horizontal - lines running along it, transoms, each position a HEIGHT above its BASE. `positions` is MILLIMETRES, digits only (D-71), commas between - "900, 2700" - or "equal 6": six equal panels that way, so five lines. The start and the base are the edges of the wall's own grid. Each position sits at least 100 mm inside those edges, because a number typed in metres - 1.2 for 1200 - would otherwise put a line 1.2 mm from one; at most 100 lines in one call, and equal panels no narrower than 100 mm. Any refusal refuses the whole request, before anything is written. **A LINE ALREADY THERE IS NOT DOUBLED.** A position within 5 mm of a line the wall already has that way - its type's, or one added before - is skipped and named in `skipped`; a position asked twice is added once. **EQUAL PANELS MEANS EQUAL PANELS.** "equal 6" on a wall that already has lines that way which do not fall on the sixths is refused, naming them - adding five more would not make six panels. Lines already on the sixths are skipped, and a result that is not six panels stops the call. **REVIT'S U AND V ARE NOT TAKEN ON TRUST.** Revit adds a line as a U line or a V line, and its reference does not say which is vertical on a wall. The choice comes from this wall's own lines; on a wall with none, from SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID's proof - Project2, Revit 2024, where a wall's vertical lines came back in Revit's V set. Each new line must then run the way asked and sit within 1 mm of the position asked, or the call stops and nothing is kept. **MULLIONS ARE OPTIONAL AND NAMED.** `mullionType` names a mullion type the model holds - "Rectangular Mullion : 50 x 150mm", with or without the space before the colon, or the bare type name when no other mullion type shares it. Compared exactly, capitals included. A name that matches none is refused WITH THE MULLION TYPES THE MODEL HAS; one that matches two is refused naming both (D-54). Nothing is loaded. Left out, blank or "none": grid lines alone. Mullions go on all segments of each new line - unless Revit has already put some there, which are named and left; changing a mullion's type is CHANGE_ELEMENT_TYPE's. ASSUMPTION for the proof: whether Revit puts the wall type's own interior mullions on a line added by hand has not been measured; the first run records it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Every refusal is made before the first write. A line or a mullion Revit will not take, a line that runs the wrong way or sits in the wrong place, or a wall Revit cannot rebuild, stops the call, and nothing it did is kept. In a shared model, a wall another user holds is refused naming them.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **direction** - text<br>**positions** - text<br>**mullion type** - text; optional, left out means *none* |
| **You get** | added, mullions added, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `ADD_CURTAIN_GRID_LINES` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"divide this curtain wall into six panels"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
5. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"add a grid line at 1200 from the bottom of this curtain wall"* · *"add vertical grid lines at 900 and 2700 on just this wall"*

<a id="add-stairs-landing"></a>

### Add stairs landing

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** add a landing between two runs of a stair that is already in the model.

Adds a landing between two runs of a stair by component already in the model - Revit's own landing between two picked runs, of the landing type the stair type names. The two runs must be of one stair; a pair Revit says it cannot join is refused before the stair is opened, and nothing changes. The new landing's depth, thickness and height are read back in mm, with the stair's riser count before and after.

<a id="attach-columns"></a>

### Attach columns

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-14 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** attach the tops or bases of these columns to the roof, floor, beam or footing selected with them, or detach them - Modify Column > Attach Top/Base, Detach Top/Base.

Attaches the tops or bases of structural and architectural columns to the roof, floor, ceiling, beam or footing selected with them - Revit's Attach Top/Base - or detaches them. Each column takes the one selected target over or under it; a target Revit does not accept is refused by name, and a column already attached to that target is left alone. Says per column what happened and why.

<a id="change-element-type"></a>

### Change element type

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** swap these elements to a different type.

Changes which type an element is - swapping every 600x600 diffuser on a floor for a different one, moving a run onto a different duct type, replacing a discontinued fitting. **The new type is an input and is never guessed.** Revit accepts a type change it cannot really honour, and the result is not an error - it is geometry that looks wrong on a drawing nobody re-checks. **Revit will accept the call and leave the element on its old type.** This is the case worth knowing: `ChangeTypeId` throws for some mismatches and, for others, simply does not take. So the type is read back after the change and only a real move is counted - the same read-back the parameter path needed after Revit returned TRUE and stored something else. Version 2 takes the type from an element as well - the one selected, its type the one the others take, another category refused - and says that only the type changed. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **new type id** - the NAME of the thing, never its number - "Level 1" for a levelId. The field's own name says which kind; optional, left out means *none*<br>**type from** - text; optional, left out means *none* |
| **You get** | changed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `CHANGE_ELEMENT_TYPE` |

**How to use it**

2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.

Other ways to ask: *"swap them to a different type"* · *"change these to the other family type"*

<a id="check-rebar-against-spec"></a>

### Check rebar against spec

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-17 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** compare the placed reinforcement with the spec values handed in, and say for each value whether it meets it.

Compares the bars placed in concrete beams, columns, footings, slabs and walls with the values of a structural spec handed in - bar count and bar type at the bottom, top and side faces of a beam or as a column's main bars, link bar type, largest link spacing and link hook angle, the cover set on the host face by face, minimum lap and anchorage as millimetres or as a multiple of d, and the longest bar allowed - and gives each value back, host by host, as meets, does not meet, or not checked with the reason. A value the spec does not give is not checked. How far a bar reaches into its support is never passed - Revit does not hold the support - so its hooks and its length outside the host are set beside the spec's figure for the engineer. Meeting a value is not a judgement that the reinforcement is adequate.

| | |

| **Kind** | Answers a question (`READ`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **bottom bars** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**top bars** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**side bars** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**main bars** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**links** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**link hook** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**cover** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**lap** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**anchorage** - text; optional, left out means *not given*<br>**max bar length** - text; optional, left out means *not given* |
| **You get** | meets, does not meet, not checked, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `CHECK_REBAR_AGAINST_SPEC` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"check anchorage and bar length"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
4. Heron answers in the chat. Nothing in the model changes.

Other ways to ask: *"a checklist for anchorage, terminations and bar-length limits"*

<a id="convert-cad-to-directshape"></a>

### Convert CAD to directshape

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** the contractor sent a 3D dwg and revit treats it as one lump.

Turns the solids inside an imported CAD file into real Revit elements - one element per solid, in a category you choose. **AN IMPORTED CAD IS ONE ELEMENT HOLDING EVERYTHING, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS USELESS UNTIL THIS IS DONE.** It has no category per piece, no parameters, nothing to schedule, and a clash check can only ever say *"something in the DWG"* - never which pipe. Once each solid is its own element in a real category, every other fragment in this library works on it: filters, colours, schedules, clash checks, parameters. **THE CATEGORY IS THE CALLER'S AND IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS.** It is what every later filter, schedule and view filter will find these by. Not every category accepts one of these elements, and one that does not is refused up front rather than per solid. **NOTHING IS DELETED.** The import stays where it is. Converting is additive, so the two sets of geometry overlap until somebody decides which to keep - and that decision is not one to make inside a conversion. **A SOLID WITH NO VOLUME IS NOT AN ELEMENT.** A CAD file carries surfaces, lines and degenerate shells as well as solids. Only real solids are converted, and how many were skipped is reported: a file that yields five elements from a hundred pieces was probably exported as surfaces, which is a conversation with whoever sent it rather than a bug here. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a whole import is one undo entry.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **category** - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused |
| **You get** | created |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `CONVERT_CAD_TO_DIRECTSHAPE` |

Once it is proved, you will ask: *"turn the cad import into real elements"* · *"the dwg is one lump in revit"* · *"make direct shapes from this cad"*

<a id="create-floor"></a>

### Create floor

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-21 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a floor slab over this area.

Creates a floor from a closed boundary on one level. The slab everything else sits on, and the thing MEP has to penetrate. **A CEILING OR A FLAT ROOF FROM THE SAME BOUNDARY (version 3)** - the type decides. A ceiling type makes a ceiling at a height above the level, read back; Revit 2020 and 2021 cannot make one from code, and say so - draw one by hand. A roof type makes a footprint roof, left flat: no slope is set on any edge, and its size and height are measured back. **The creation call changed at Revit 2022 and this fragment still runs on 2020.** The old one took a curve array through the document's creation object; the new one is a static taking curve loops. Neither name can appear in source that compiles at both ends, so whichever exists is found at run time - the same shape as CREATE_CEILING, for the same reason. **The base height is the level's PROJECT elevation.** Every XYZ the API takes is project-internal, while `Elevation` is measured from whatever the level type's Elevation Base says. On a model set out to a survey datum the two differ, and the wrong one puts the slab at the wrong height with no error at all. **The boundary closes itself** and must not cross itself. A self-crossing loop is refused by Revit, and that refusal is reported rather than swallowed. **AN EDGE CAN BE AN ARC (version 2, row 5b-1216).** `arc MX,MY X,Y` after a corner makes the next edge an arc: through MX,MY, ending at X,Y - the writing CREATE_FAMILY_FORMS's loops take, so one writing works for a family and a project. A round slab is two arcs, the second ending where the first began; a boundary with an arc in it may end on its first corner, because a round one has to. A boundary with no `arc` in it makes exactly the floor version 1 made, and a last corner repeating the first is still refused there. An arc whose three points are in a line, or two in one place, makes nothing. **It makes one floor, not a storey.** Openings, shafts and penetrations are separate jobs; nothing here cuts a hole in anything. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | created, edges, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |

<a id="create-from-room-boundaries"></a>

### Create from room boundaries

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).** Held on purpose: Back to DRAFT on 2026-11-16, on the owner's answer to row 5b-1643: the 2026-10-21 proof ran a floor and made no wall finish, the one thing version 2 added. NEEDS-CHECKING Group HX's HX1 to HX3, then a new proof whose positive case makes wall finishes, before it is PROVEN again.

**What it does:** put a ceiling or a floor in every room, the shape of the room, or line its walls with a finish.

Builds new floors, ceilings or wall finishes room by room, each one the shape of its room - the room's own boundary gives the outline, holes included, so no coordinates are typed. The type given decides what is made: a floor type makes floors, a ceiling type makes ceilings, and a wall type lines the room's walls with a thin new wall of plaster, tile or cladding, to a height. There is no mode to get wrong, and a type that is none of the three is refused before anything is attempted. **THE HOLES ARE THE REASON THIS EXISTS.** A room's boundary comes back as several loops: the first is the outside edge and every one after it is a shaft, a core or a column the room wraps around. Building from the first loop alone puts a slab straight over the shaft - which looks right in plan, passes every check, and is found by the person who tries to run a riser through it. The plain creators take ONE loop and say so; this is the fragment for the real-room case. **AN UNENCLOSED ROOM HAS NO USABLE BOUNDARY.** It reports no area and no loops, so nothing can be built on it. Those rooms are named rather than silently skipped - a floor of thirty rooms that produced twenty-eight ceilings needs to say which two. **A WALL TYPE LINES THE ROOM'S WALLS (version 2).** Every edge of the room that is a wall gets a thin wall of that type on the wall's INSIDE face, from the room's floor plus `baseOffset` up to `heightAboveLevel` above the room's floor (its level plus the room's own Base Offset), with its exterior side, where the first layer of a finish type sits, facing the room. Neighbouring finishes meet at the corners. `joinToHost` joins each one to the wall behind it. Straight walls and arc walls alike. **A SECOND RUN LAYS A SECOND FINISH OVER THE FIRST.** Finishes are not room bounding, so the room's boundary cannot show they are already there: look for walls of the finish type in the room before running it again. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). **THE FINISH STOPS AT EVERY OPENING IN THE WALL BEHIND.** Across every door, window, wall opening and embedded curtain wall in the host wall, the finish is built only above and below it - a gap to the floor at a door with the finish carried on above its head, the finish kept below a sill and above a head - so a finish is several walls, never one with an opening cut in it. **THE ROOM'S AREA DOES NOT MOVE.** Every finish is made NOT room bounding, so the room's area and every schedule reading it are unchanged. **WHAT IS NOT LINED IS NAMED, NEVER PASSED OVER.** A curtain wall, a room or space separation line, a wall in a linked model (its doors cannot be read from here), a column or anything else that is not a wall, and an edge neither straight nor an arc are each skipped, totalled by reason in `skippedSummary` and in each room's line of `finishSummary`. A room with no usable boundary is in `unenclosed`, as for floors and ceilings.

| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **host type** - by name, as Revit writes it<br>**height above level** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**base offset** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm; optional, left out means *0*<br>**rooms** - text; optional, left out means *all*<br>**join to host** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | created, with holes, finish walls, finish summary |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `CREATE_FROM_ROOM_BOUNDARIES` |

<a id="create-opening"></a>

### Create opening

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-14 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** cut the hole through this wall or slab - or the opening in a wall- or ceiling-based family's own template wall or ceiling.

Cuts an opening through a host element - a wall, a floor, a roof or a ceiling - from a closed boundary, and through a beam, brace or column with Revit's own framing opening. **A WALL** (version 4, 2026-11-02) takes Revit's own wall opening - an upright rectangle, `wallOpening` "1200 x 800 at 900": width, height and sill above the wall's base level, in millimetres, centred on the wall unless "along 2500" says where. Boundary points on a wall must be one rectangle's corners. A curved or curtain wall is refused by name. Read back: its size and sill, to a millimetre. **A BEAM, BRACE OR COLUMN** (version 2, 2026-10-12, the gap fill) takes the framing opening: perpendicularFace true cuts through the web, false through the flanges - the duct or pipe penetration through a steel beam's web. **IN A WALL- OR CEILING-BASED FAMILY (version 3, 2026-11-01)** - the Opening tool those templates offer, CREATE_FAMILY_HOST_OPENING's job, merged in: `shape` is ONE closed loop in millimetres in the template's own wall or ceiling - along the wall and up it, X,Y in plan for a ceiling - and the template's one wall or ceiling is found, so `host` and `boundary` are left out. An opening cut there is cut in every wall or ceiling the family is placed on. A floor- or roof-based family is refused by name - Revit's call takes a wall or a ceiling. Its size is FIXED as drawn, and the answer says so. Read back, all or nothing: its host and its extent, to a millimetre. **THIS IS THE HALF `PROPOSE_MEP_OPENINGS` SAYS SOMEBODY ELSE MUST DO, AND NOBODY DID.** Its own purpose reads: *"It creates nothing... The list this produces is meant to be read, argued with, and only then acted on - by a separate write that somebody approved."* Measured 2026-09-18: that write did not exist anywhere in the library. So Heron could find every place the services pass through structure, size each hole, audit the holes already cut and check their sleeves - and could not cut one. **THE SPLIT IS RIGHT AND IS KEPT.** Proposing and cutting stay two operations, because cutting holes in somebody's structure is not a thing to do as a side effect of looking for them. This fragment is the deliberate second step, run on a list a person has seen. **THE BOUNDARY IS IN THE HOST'S PLANE AND THE CALLER OWNS IT.** Revit projects the profile onto the host; a boundary worked out against the wrong face comes back as an opening in the wrong place rather than as an error. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a run of forty penetrations is one undo entry.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **host** - ONE PARTICULAR element - SELECT IT IN REVIT and type `selected`. Exactly one: none or several are refused, and so is a typed name, because an instance has no name of its own; optional<br>**boundary** - points - MILLIMETRES, "x,y,z"; several separated by semicolons - "0,0,0; 5000,0,0"; optional<br>**perpendicular face** - yes or no - true or false; optional<br>**shape** - text; optional, left out means *none*<br>**wall opening** - text; optional, left out means *none* |
| **You get** | created, opening id, built, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `CREATE_OPENING` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.

### Create shaped stairs

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make an L-shaped, U-shaped or spiral stair from one level to another, placed from a point, turning left or right at its landing.

Makes a Revit stair by component - an L-shaped stair with a landing at the turn, a U-shaped stair with a landing across its end, or a spiral stair - from a base level to a top level, placed from a point on plan: the middle of the first riser for an L or U, the centre for a spiral. The first run climbs north, south, east or west and turns left or right. The riser count comes from the stair type's Maximum Riser Height and its tread from the type's Minimum Tread Depth; the type is the one named, or Revit's default for new stairs, said in the answer. A landing depth in mm sets the landing; without one Revit makes its own. What Revit made is read back - risers, tread, runs, landings and the landing's depth - and a stair Revit refuses is refused with its reason and leaves nothing. Or a stair by sketch: one run from its two boundaries and its risers.

<a id="create-stairs"></a>

### Create stairs

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make a stair between these two levels in this stair hall.

Makes a real Revit stair - a Stairs element with its runs and landing - from a base level to a top level, laid out inside a rectangle on plan: one straight run, or a U (dogleg) with a landing across the far end. Optionally cuts the opening in the top level's floor over it. **NOTHING IN THE LIBRARY COULD MAKE A STAIR BEFORE THIS, AND NO FRAGMENT COULD.** Revit makes a stair only inside a StairsEditScope, which refuses to start while a transaction is open - and every write fragment runs inside one. Measured 2026-10-03 on Project2, Revit 2024. This fragment declares the ambient `editScopeFailures` need, and D-112 has the add-in run it inside the job's TransactionGroup with no transaction open: still one undo, still rolled back on a preview. **THE RISER HEIGHT AND TREAD ARE THE STAIR TYPE'S.** The riser count is the fewest that keeps every riser at or under the type's Maximum Riser Height; the tread is its Minimum Tread Depth. A type name that is not loaded is refused, with the loaded names listed - never guessed. **THE RECTANGLE IS THE CLEAR INSIDE OF THE HALL**, wall faces and not centrelines. `entrySide` is the side the first riser faces - the stair climbs away from it - and `startOffset` is the clear floor between that side and the first riser: where a door opens, and on a U where the top run arrives. **ALL OR NOTHING, READ BACK.** The run count, the landing, the total risers and the stair's plan extent inside the rectangle are read inside the edit scope, and any miss cancels it. With `cutOpening` the top level's slab is cut over the stair and its VOLUME read before and after; an opening that removed nothing takes the stair away again. **THE OPENING IS THE SLAB'S OWN, NOT A SHAFT.** Measured 2026-10-03, rolled back: a shaft from Level 1 to Level 2 over the hall removed nothing from either slab, while a floor opening in the Level 2 slab removed 8 m3. Revit gives the stair the model's default stair railing on both sides as it is made (5b-455); this adds none of its own, and reads them back.

<a id="create-wall"></a>

### Create wall

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-01 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** build a wall between these two points, straight or along an arc.

Creates walls between consecutive points on one level, at a given height - straight, or along an arc where one is written. The plain "put a wall here" - the thing rooms are bounded by and MEP has to pass through. **Written as a run of points, like CREATE_MEP_RUNS.** Two points is the single-wall case. A room needs four walls and a corridor needs two, so making the run the general form saves the caller a loop and keeps the whole library one shape. **AN ARC IS WRITTEN IN THE RUN (version 2, row 5b-1216).** `arc MX,MY X,Y` after a point makes the next wall an arc: through MX,MY, ending at X,Y - the writing CREATE_FAMILY_FORMS's loops take, so one writing works for a family and a project. A full circle is two arcs. Basic and curtain walls alike; how a curtain wall's panels sit on the arc is Revit's, and is recorded by the first run (NEEDS-CHECKING Group HM), not claimed here. A run with no `arc` in it builds exactly what version 1 built. An arc whose three points are in a line, or two in one place, refuses the whole run: nothing is built, because the next wall would start where the bad one ends. **The base height is the level's PROJECT elevation.** Every XYZ the API takes is project-internal, while `Elevation` is measured from whatever the level type's Elevation Base says. On a model set out to a survey datum the two differ, and the wrong one builds the wall at the wrong height with no error. **A WALL CAN START ABOVE ITS LEVEL (version 3, row 5b-1345)** - Revit's Base Offset, in millimetres: a crown post that starts part-way up a storey, a wall on a sill. Left out it is 0, and the wall is version 2's to the word. The height is measured from there, as Revit measures Unconnected Height: 1500 up and 3000 high stands from 1500 to 4500 above the level. Each wall's offset is read back off the wall and said. **The height is unconnected.** The wall stands at the height given and is not attached to the level above. Attaching it is a separate parameter change and is not done here, because "up to the slab" and "3 m tall" are different instructions. **Nothing is joined.** Walls meeting at a corner are not joined to each other by this, and whether Revit joins them itself is not claimed. JOIN_GEOMETRY is what makes two elements agree about which cuts which. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="delete-elements"></a>

### Delete elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** delete these elements from the model.

Deletes elements. The most destructive thing in this library, and the one whose honest reporting matters most. **Deleting one element can delete others, and Revit will not warn first.** A wall takes its hosted doors and windows. A duct run takes its fittings and its insulation. A level can take everything on it. `Document.Delete` hands back **what actually went** — which is routinely a longer list than what was asked for — and that returned set, never the input count, is what this fragment reports. **So the caller can tell the user what will really happen before it happens.** This is what makes Golden Rule 17's preview possible for deletion: run the same call inside a transaction that is rolled back, and the returned set is the true blast radius. **A WALL ATTACHED TO A ROOF, FLOOR OR CEILING THAT GOES IS DETACHED, AND NAMED** (version 2). It is changed, not deleted, so `deleted` never shows it. So before the delete every wall attached at its top or base and lying in plan under what is deleted is named, and after it each is read again: `detachedWalls` lists those whose attachment went, and `wallsNote` says what that means - on Revit 2020 to 2024 Heron cannot attach a wall again, so it is Attach Top/Base by hand. **WHAT WENT IS NAMED, BY CATEGORY** (version 3). Each delete is first tried inside a SubTransaction that is rolled back, and every id that trial returns is read while it is still in the model. `deletedWhat` names every deleted id - category, name, and why it went (asked for, went with an element, or a form's own sketch) - and `deletedByCategory` says what was asked for and what also went, counted by category. In a family, a form's own sketch, sketch plane and sketch lines are counted together, so 241 reads as "21 form(s) + their sketches". An id it could not read is NOT READ. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | deleted, also went, detached walls, deleted what |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `DELETE_ELEMENTS` |

<a id="disallow-join"></a>

### Disallow join

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-12 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** stop these walls cleaning up into each other at the ends.

Turns automatic end-joining off - or back on - for walls and structural framing. Revit's own *Disallow Join*, in bulk: the fix for walls that clean up into each other where they should read as separate, and for beams whose ends get eaten by the column they run into. **A PINNED ELEMENT REFUSES SILENTLY, AND THAT IS THE STEP EVERYONE MISSES.** The join calls do not throw on a pinned wall. They return normally and change nothing, so a script reports success on a model it never touched. Pinned elements are unpinned first and pinned back afterwards, and how many were pinned is reported - the number is otherwise invisible, and its absence is what makes this look like a Revit bug. **WALLS AND BEAMS ARE TWO DIFFERENT CALLS AND THERE IS NO SHARED ONE.** Anything that is neither is named as unsupported rather than quietly skipped, because a selection is usually mixed and "it did nothing" is not an answer. **WHICH END IS 0 AND WHICH IS 1 DEPENDS ON HOW THE WALL WAS DRAWN.** They are the start and finish of the location curve, and nothing on screen says which is which - so `whichEnd` exists, and "both" is the answer that does what somebody pointing at a corner means. **TURNING IT BACK ON IS A REAL CHANGE TOO.** Re-allowing a join lets Revit clean the corner up again, which can visibly move where a wall ends. It is the same call in reverse and it is reported the same way. Every element is read back afterwards, so what is reported is the join state the model actually has. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="duplicate-type"></a>

### Duplicate type

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a new type from the type these are using.

Duplicates the TYPE behind the elements handed in, under a new name - *"make a new duct type at 300 wide"*, *"I need a copy of this wall type"*. The new type is created and nothing else happens: no instance is moved onto it and no size is set on it. **It refuses when the selection sits on more than one type**, and that refusal is the fragment's main decision. The earlier library let one literal name be applied to every distinct type found; Revit requires type names to be unique, so the first duplicate succeeded and the rest quietly did not - a batch that reports success and half-happened. So the distinct types are counted first, and if there is more than one they are NAMED and nothing is created. The user then narrows the selection, which is the answer they wanted anyway. **A type handed in is the type duplicated** (version 2) - a door type picked in the Project Browser or by SELECT_TYPES, with no door placed - and so is one named as *"Family: Type"*, *"copy M_Single-Flush: 0915 x 2134mm as 1000 x 2134mm"*. **Forty instances of one type give ONE new type, not forty.** The types are de-duplicated before anything is created. **Two steps have to follow it and neither is guessed.** A duplicated type is an exact copy - same size, same everything - so WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS sets what makes it different, and CHANGE_ELEMENT_TYPE moves instances onto it if that is wanted. Doing either from here would mean deciding, on somebody's behalf, that their existing elements should change. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="edit-curtain-grid-segments"></a>

### Edit curtain grid segments

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** remove a grid line from this one curtain wall, or take out or put back one segment of it - Revit's Add/Remove Segments.

TAKES A CURTAIN GRID LINE AWAY from ONE curtain wall - the one picked in Revit - or takes out one or more of its SEGMENTS, the pieces between the lines that cross it, or puts back segments taken out before. Revit's own Add/Remove Segments tool and deleting a grid line, typed: "remove the vertical grid line at 3000 on this curtain wall", "cut that grid line out of the bottom panel only", "put back the segment I removed". **THIS WALL ONLY.** The change is on the wall's own curtain grid; nothing on its family type is written, so no other wall changes with it. SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID is the one that changes a type's layout for all its walls. ADD_CURTAIN_GRID_LINES adds new lines. **ONE STRAIGHT CURTAIN WALL AT A TIME.** Exactly one among what is handed in; anything else that is not a curtain wall is named in `notCurtain` and left alone; two curtain walls are refused; a curved one is refused. **A LINE IS NAMED BY WHERE IT IS.** `direction` vertical - a line running up the wall, `lineAt` its distance ALONG the wall from its START - or horizontal - a transom, `lineAt` its HEIGHT above the BASE. Millimetres, digits only, commas between, measured off the grid's own edges, the way ADD_CURTAIN_GRID_LINES places a line; a line within 5 mm is that line. A position with no line there refuses the whole call, naming where the lines that way are. **A SEGMENT IS NAMED BY A POINT ON IT.** `segmentsAt` left out or "all": the whole line. Otherwise millimetres on the line - a height on a vertical line, a distance from the start on a horizontal one - and each picks the segment whose span holds it. A point on the joint between two segments is refused, because which one was meant cannot be told. Naming every segment a line has left is refused: say "all" to take the line away. **`action` remove or restore.** Left out it is remove. Remove with "all" deletes the line, and the mullions on it go with it, counted; remove with points takes those segments out. Restore with "all" puts every segment taken out back; restore with points puts those back. A segment already the way asked is skipped and named, never counted. **A PINNED LINE IS REFUSED, BY NAME.** The lines a curtain wall type lays out arrive pinned to it; taking one away or apart changes what the type drew on this wall, so it is a deliberate act - SET_PIN_STATE unpins it first, or SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID changes the type for every wall. ASSUMPTION for the proof: that a type's own lines read pinned through the API as they show the pin in Revit. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Every refusal is made before the first write. After one regeneration every change is read back off the wall - a deleted line no longer there, a removed segment among the skipped ones, a restored one among the existing - and one that is not stops the call, and nothing it did is kept. In a shared model a wall another user holds is refused naming them.

<a id="extend-roof-to-roof"></a>

### Extend roof to roof

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** lengthen a roof by extrusion: move its Extrusion Start or End until its end reaches a sloped roof face, measured with rays.

Extends a roof by extrusion until its end meets the upper face of another roof. Two roofs are handed in. Rays are cast from the corners and edge points of each end of the roof by extrusion toward the other roof alone, in the 3D view given; a hit counts only on a face that looks up, and the farthest hit is how far the end has to go. Without maxExtendMm it measures, says the distance and changes nothing; with it, the end is moved by changing Extrusion Start or End, when the distance is within the limit, and read back off the roof's geometry. The end is flat, so it goes to its farthest point and elsewhere further - through the other roof and under it; cleaning the overlap is offered as the next step, and the part under the other roof stays, said. From Revit 2022 a roof by footprint's gable end is moved the same way, in sketch edit mode; on 2020 and 2021 the answer names the release and says it is done by hand. Two ends that both meet are not chosen between. The other roof must show in the 3D view: rays only see what the view shows.

<a id="extract-cad-curves"></a>

### Extract CAD curves

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** turn the lines on a CAD layer into real revit lines.

Reads the geometry of an imported or linked CAD file and redraws the curves on chosen layers as real Revit model lines or detail lines - the "trace this DWG background into Revit" job, done by reading it rather than by drawing over it. With listOnly it hands back the segments' coordinates instead and draws nothing (version 2). **NAMING NO LAYER SURVEYS; NAMING LAYERS EXTRACTS.** With an empty layer list this creates nothing and reports every layer it found with a curve count against each. That is the opposite of the obvious default, on purpose: a drawing's layer names cannot be guessed, they are case-sensitive, and "all layers" on a survey drawing is tens of thousands of lines nobody asked for. So one run tells you what is there, and the second run asks for it by name. **Layer names are matched exactly, including case.** A CAD layer is whatever the other office typed. Matching loosely would quietly pull in a neighbouring layer, and the survey above is what makes exact matching workable. **Only flat curves are taken, and the rest are counted.** A model line needs a sketch plane and a detail line lives in one view; a curve whose two ends differ in height belongs to neither. Those are reported rather than dropped, because a survey drawing with levels baked into it produces almost nothing and the count is the only clue why. **Polylines become straight segments, and splines and ellipses are refused.** A polyline is already a chain of straight pieces and comes across exactly. A spline is not, and approximating one silently would put linework in a Revit model that does not match the drawing it came from. **There is a cap on how many lines one run creates**, and it is reported when it bites. A traced layer that turns out to hold 40,000 segments should stop and say so rather than fill the model. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Golden Rule 17's preview - run it, look, roll back - is how to see the result before keeping it.

| **You get** | created, layer counts, coordinates, findings |

<a id="filter-elements-by-category"></a>

### Filter elements by category

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** all elements of one category in the active document.

Answers "which elements" for one Revit category or several, in the active document, excluding types, optionally scoped to one level. It is the filter half of every "select the X" and "how many X" job, which is exactly why it is a fragment and not part of either: two questions sharing one filter is D-29's design working. Leave levelId out, or pass none, for the whole model. Reports unresolvedLevel - how many elements had NO level found at all - so a broken level lookup reads as "12 found, 12 with no level" instead of as a plausible zero. Silently dropping them is what makes that failure invisible. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. Each link is asked for the category, and for the level by the host level's NAME - a link's levels are its own - and its matches are counted per link in `linkedMatches`. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements` stays this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 3 - version 2 read the links - and version 1's proof no longer describes the code; version 3's does. **SEVERAL CATEGORIES, OR ONE VIEW (version 4).** `categories` names several in one pass, `perCategory` shows each - one asked for and empty at 0 - and `inViewOnly` narrows it to what one view draws. `categoryName` takes a category by the name the model holds - an imported CAD file's too - and a name that matches none comes back with its near misses, nothing read. **A LEVEL OR A VIEW WITHOUT A CATEGORY, AND WHAT IS NOT THERE (version 5).** "What is on level 2" and "what is showing on this view" need no category. `withoutLevel` gives the elements on no level; `notShowingIn` what the model holds that a view does not show. **WHAT HAS NO LEVEL, ACROSS THE MODEL (version 6).** `withoutLevel` with no category is answered over the model categories alone - never the views, sheets and materials that rightly have no level.

The field's own name says which kind; optional, left out means *none*<br>**in view only** - a view, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused; optional<br>**not showing in** - a view, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused; optional<br>**without level** - yes or no - true or false; optional<br>**cut by view** - yes or no - true or false; optional<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |

<a id="filter-elements-in-room"></a>

### Filter elements in room

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which of these elements are inside this room.

Narrows a set of elements to the ones inside a given room. The filter every room-based MEP job needs — terminals in this room, the fittings in this room, sprinklers in this room, what is served by this space — and nothing here could do it. **A room is a VOLUME, not a rectangle.** An L-shaped room's bounding box covers ground that is not in the room, and a bounding-box test puts the neighbour's diffuser in your schedule. Revit's own point-in-room test is used instead, which follows the real boundary. **It tests ONE point per element, and says so.** A duct crossing three rooms belongs to whichever room contains the point tested. That is the honest limit: deciding how much of a duct must be inside to count is a question about the job — a takeoff wants length per room, a terminal count wants the point — and a fragment that chose would be silently wrong for the other. **The room's own level is not a filter.** A room is a volume with a height, so an element above the ceiling can be genuinely inside it, and excluding by level would drop exactly the services somebody is asking about. **Version 2: a door or window in a wall goes by its From and To instead.**

<a id="flip-elements"></a>

### Flip elements

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** turn these family instances round using their own flip controls.

Flips the hand or facing of family instances - a door swinging the wrong way, a diffuser or a piece of equipment pointing the wrong direction. It is Revit's own flip arrows, done to many elements at once. This is NOT rotation. A flip uses the family's own built-in controls and respects how the family was authored; rotating 180 degrees moves geometry and can leave a hosted element wrong against its host. When somebody says *"it is the wrong way round"* about a door or a diffuser, this is usually what they mean. Not every family can flip, and the ones that cannot are reported rather than attempted - a family author decides whether a flip control exists at all. **VERSION 2: A FLIPPED DOOR'S FROM AND TO ROOM FOLLOW ITS SWING.** Revit leaves From Room and To Room as they were when a door's facing is flipped, so they are left the wrong way round. After a facing flip the door's To Room is swapped to the room it now swings into - only where the rooms either side say so - and each door is named. `fromToRoomOnly` fixes the From and To Room of doors already wrong, and flips nothing. **VERSION 3: A WORK-PLANE-BASED PART CAN FLIP ITS WORK PLANE.** A nested part placed on a plane facing the wrong way comes in facing inward and upside down, and no hand or facing flip turns it. `flipWorkPlane` flips each part's work plane where Revit allows it, and says which way it now faces and where it now sits. One that cannot is named and left. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

**"THE ARROWS ARE WRONG" MEANS TWO DIFFERENT JOBS AND ONE OF THEM CHANGES THE MODEL:** | What you meant | Use | |---|---| | "is the flow going the right way", "are the arrows pointing the right way" - to check | `CHECK_FLOW_DIRECTION`, read-only | | "the diffuser is the wrong way round", "turn it around" - to change | `FLIP_ELEMENTS`, which flips real elements | A question about direction must never flip anything. Both fragments carry this table - written one way it only routes whoever lands on the newer file.

<a id="join-geometry"></a>

### Join geometry

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** join these walls and floors together so they cut each other.

Joins - or unjoins - the geometry of many elements with one target, so they cut each other properly instead of overlapping. The wall-meets-slab, column-in-wall, beam-into-column job, and the fix for a section that shows a double line where two elements share the same space. **Until this existed, "join these walls together" resolved to the MEP fitting fragment**, and after that to the one joining open MEP connectors - two writes on ducts and pipes answering a question about walls. Both would have found nothing to do and reported it, which is the quiet kind of wrong. **Joining is not touching, and it is not a clash.** Two elements can overlap in space and be unjoined - Revit then draws both, and the section shows the line through the middle. FIND_CLASHES reports the overlap; this makes them agree about which one wins. **Many to one, because that is the shape the job takes.** Twelve beams into one column, a batch of walls into one slab. Joining pairs within a set is a different question and this does not guess at it. **A pair Revit will not join is counted, not thrown.** Elements that do not actually touch, and categories Revit refuses to join, are normal outcomes rather than errors - and a batch must not lose the eleven that worked because the twelfth would not. **Order matters in Revit and is not silently chosen here.** Which element cuts which is decided by the join order, and this fragment does not reverse it. What it does report is which pairs were ALREADY joined, because re-joining them would do nothing and counting them as work would be a lie. Version 2 refuses by id the same element on both sides of a pair - the target handed in among the elements - and says that quantities have moved whenever a pair was joined or unjoined. Version 3 adds join switch, which reverses an existing join. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

### List materials

**What it does:** every material this project or family holds, by name, with its class.

Counts and lists everything the Material Browser shows for the document Heron is working on - a project, or a family open in the Family Editor: how many there are, and each one's name, class (Metal, Concrete, Plastic) and element id, sorted by name. **IT LISTS WHAT THE DOCUMENT HOLDS, NOT WHAT IS USED.** One read, and nothing else. Whether anything uses an entry means walking every element, every type and every painted face - FIND_PURGEABLE_ELEMENTS' walk with includeMaterials (FIND_UNUSED_MATERIALS' until 2026-11-01), not repeated here. **A FAMILY'S LIST IS THE FAMILY'S OWN.** In the Family Editor the answer is what that family carries, never what a project it is loaded into holds, nor another document open beside it. A chat reads the model it is pinned to, and the answer says so. **WITH ITS ASSETS, WHEN ASKED** (version 2, 2026-10-13, the gap fill): `withAssets` adds every number of each material's physical and thermal asset - density, conductivity, specific heat - as Revit formats it in the project's units, so no unit is converted here. **EVERY TAB, WHEN ASKED** (version 3): `withAllTabs` reads each one's identity, graphics and render appearance in one line - and which have no appearance at all; `withLibraryAppearances` lists the appearance assets Revit's library holds. **THE TEXTURE FILES, WHEN ASKED** (version 5): `withTextures` lists the image files each appearance uses, slot by slot, with whether each file is there, and names the missing ones; `onlyMissing` lists only those. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

| **You get** | material count, material list, material classes, material ids, library appearances, textures, missing, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |

<a id="move-curtain-grid-line"></a>

### Move curtain grid line

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** move this mullion, or the curtain grid line it sits on, along one curtain wall - by a distance or to a position.

MOVES A CURTAIN GRID LINE ON ONE CURTAIN WALL, and the mullions on it and the panels either side with it - Revit's Move on a curtain grid line, typed: "move this mullion 300 mm", "move the grid line at 1500 to 1800", "shift this transom up 200". **A MULLION IS MOVED BY ITS GRID LINE.** In Revit a mullion follows the grid line under it, so a mullion handed in names the line of the same wall that runs its way within 5 mm of it, and that line moves. A mullion on the wall's border sits on no grid line: named in `notMovable`, never moved. A grid line can be handed in itself, or the curtain wall with `direction` and `lineAt` naming the line by where it is, the way ADD_CURTAIN_GRID_LINES places one. Everything handed in must be on ONE straight curtain wall. **`move` IS A DISTANCE OR A PLACE, IN MILLIMETRES.** "300" or "+300" moves each line 300 mm toward the wall's END (the end it was drawn to) for a vertical line, or UP for a horizontal one; "-300" the other way; "to 1800" puts ONE line 1800 mm along from the grid's start, or above its base. Left and right depend on the view, so they are never taken. **NO LINE ONTO OR PAST ANOTHER, NONE AT THE EDGE.** A move that would put a line onto or past a line that is not moving, or within 100 mm of the grid's edge, is refused before anything moves - panels would merge or change order, and a number typed in metres would move a line by a fraction of a millimetre. A PINNED line - one a curtain wall type laid out at its spacing - is refused by name: unpin it first (SET_PIN_STATE), or change the type (SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID). This wall only: nothing on its type is written. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Every refusal is made before the first write. After one regeneration every line is measured: within 1 mm of where it was sent, with the same number of mullions on it as before - or the call stops and nothing it did is kept. ASSUMPTION for the proof: that Revit's move of an unpinned grid line by the API carries its mullions as its Move tool does; the read-back settles it. In a shared model a wall another user holds is refused naming them.

<a id="place-family-instances"></a>

### Place family instances

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-23 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** place instances of one family type at these points - in a project, or nested in the family being edited.

Places one family type at a list of points on a level, and reports every point it could not place at. It is the last step of every layout job - air terminals, sprinkler heads, detectors - after something else has worked out WHERE they go. It activates the symbol first, which is the step that makes this fragment worth having: an unactivated type places nothing and says nothing. Version 4 places a family as a real structural member when asked - a column with its top level and offset, a footing - and refuses a beam or a brace. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so twenty-four sprinklers are one undo entry rather than twenty-four.

<a id="place-family-on-face"></a>

### Place family on face

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put this face-based family on that face, hosted to it properly.

Hosts a FACE-BASED family on the face it finds looking up to a ceiling, down to a floor or across to a wall - in this model or a linked one - so each instance is genuinely HOSTED by the thing it sits on. **VERSION 2 (2026-10-13) FINDS THE FACE.** Version 1 took face references, which no request can carry, so nothing could run it. Now each point looks along a direction through a 3D view, and a face in a loaded link hosts too - version 1 refused those on a belief never measured. **PLACE_FAMILY_INSTANCES CANNOT DO THIS, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS NOT COSMETIC.** That one places at a point on a level. A diffuser placed that way sits at a height that happens to look right and knows nothing about the ceiling; move the ceiling and it stays behind. Placed here it is hosted, so it moves with its host and is deleted with it. Same picture on day one, different model. **THE PLACEMENT TYPE IS CHECKED FIRST, BECAUSE THE WRONG FAMILY THROWS.** The face overload requires a work-plane-based family. Handing it a level-based one raises an exception from inside Revit that says nothing a modeller can act on, so the family is checked and refused by name instead. **A REFERENCE INTO A LINKED MODEL IS REFUSED.** You cannot host an element in this project on a face that belongs to another file - the host would be a thing this document does not own. Revit's own error for it is obscure, and the mistake is easy: the ceiling you clicked may well be in the architectural link. **THE HOST IS VERIFIED AFTER PLACING, NOT ASSUMED.** An instance that came back with no host is reported as a problem even though Revit did not complain, because an unhosted instance is exactly the failure this fragment exists to prevent and it looks completely correct on screen. **THE SYMBOL IS ACTIVATED IF IT IS NOT ALREADY.** An unactivated symbol places nothing and raises nothing - the most silent failure in the Revit API. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16). One operation is one undo entry, and the caller owns it.

| **You get** | created, placed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `PLACE_FAMILY_ON_FACE` |

<a id="place-hosted-family"></a>

### Place hosted family

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** put a door, a window, a skylight or any hosted family into its wall, floor, ceiling or roof.

Places a hosted family INTO its host at each point given: a door or a window into the wall there, and - since version 4 - a skylight into a flat roof, a roof hatch or a vent into the roof over the point, a floor drain, a grating or a floor box into the floor under it, a light or a fitting into the ceiling over it. A door is turned to swing toward the room named for it and a window to face out, and - when a sill height is given - a door's or a window's sill is set and read back. What a modeller asks it for: put doors and windows into walls, skylights into roofs, drains and floor boxes into floors, fittings into ceilings. **THE FAMILY SAYS WHAT IT GOES INTO** - its own Host setting, never its category or the words used: a skylight is a Windows family hosted by a roof. A face-based family is refused, naming PLACE_FAMILY_ON_FACE; one that is not hosted at all, naming PLACE_FAMILY_INSTANCES. **ONE ALREADY AT THE POINT IS NOT DOUBLED.** One of the same category, in the same host, within 50 mm of the point, is taken as the one asked for and set right rather than stacked on - so re-running is safe, and it is how one placed earlier gets corrected. **PLACE_FAMILY_ON_FACE IS THE OTHER HALF AND IS NOT THIS.** That one hosts to a FACE picked off geometry, which is right for a face-based family on a soffit. This one hosts to the ELEMENT - the wall, floor, ceiling or roof. **VERSION 4: FLOORS, CEILINGS AND ROOFS, AND A WINDOW FACES OUT.** The host is found straight down through the point - up, for a ceiling: floors and ceilings on `level`, roofs on every level, where `level` only decides between two. None or two there, and the point is named and skipped. Every one is read back - its host, its Level, where it stands and how it is turned - in `hostedIn` and, whole, in `readBack`. `rotation` turns it in plan, in degrees; blank leaves it as Revit places it. No offset and no sill: the host's face decides its height. `toRoomAt` and `hingeAt` are a door's and a window's and are not read for a roof, floor or ceiling - send the points again, since an empty point list is refused. A window keeps facing its wall's exterior and no hinge is read for it (rows 5b-325, 5b-293). **VERSION 3 SETS THE SILL, AND READS IT EITHER WAY.** `sillHeight` is in millimetres above the level, or blank. BLANK IS VERSION 2 EXACTLY: the sill is left as Revit placed it - but what each door or window reads is still reported, in `sills`, because a window placed through the API has been said to land with its sill at 0. Nobody here has measured that; the reading settles it either way. Given a sill: - **Checked before placing.** Level + sill + the type's Height (the built-in Height doors and windows both use) against the top of the wall found at the point. A head that would stand above the wall skips that point - `sillTooHigh` - and nothing is placed or changed there. A type whose Height is on the instance cannot be read this cheaply, and the reply counts those points as not checked rather than guessing. - **Set on the built-in Sill Height and nothing else.** A family without one, or with it read-only, is never given some other parameter found by its name - a typed name may repeat (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). One this call placed is removed again inside the same undo; one already there is left as it was. Both are named in `noSillParameter`. **A door or window already in the wall is never given the asked sill** - this call did not place it; its sill is read and said in `sills`, and nothing on it changes. - **Read back after a regenerate**, and set beside what was asked in `sills`. More than 1 mm out is named in `sillWrong`, never counted as right.

**VERSION 2'S RECORD FOLLOWS.** The two rules about a door already at the point and PLACE_FAMILY_ON_FACE are version 2's as well, and still hold. **VERSION 1 COULD NOT BE GIVEN A WALL BY NAME.** It took the host as one element, and a wall instance has no name anybody could type: the add-in refuses a typed name for one particular element, and until 2026-09-23 heron_resolve told the caller to type an element TYPE (row 5b-190). Only a wall selected by hand could reach it - one wall for every point - and it was never run. So on 2026-09-22 in Project4 a door went through PLACE_FAMILY_INSTANCES instead, which answered "placed 1, failed 0", and the door was FREE-STANDING - right in plan, cutting nothing (FRAGMENT-ISSUES, "A drawing set and a house plan", item 1). Version 2 asks each POINT which wall it sits in: the straight walls on the level whose location line passes within half their width of the point, away from their ends. One wall, and the door goes in it. None, or two equally near, and the point is named and skipped - a door is never guessed into a wall. **HOW EACH DOOR HANGS IS NAMED BY THE CALLER, NEVER ASSUMED (D-33), AND IT IS THREE SETTINGS.** Each point comes with a second point inside the room the door should swing toward, and a third on the side its hinge belongs - the side wall, when the open leaf should lie back along it. Measured 2026-09-24 in Project1 (Revit 2024), M_Single-Flush: - **The swing.** The leaf's plan swing arc lies on the door's FACING side, so the room a short way out along the facing must be the room asked for, or the door is flipped once. - **The hinge.** Read off the same plan swing arc, whose centre is the hinge, in a floor plan of the level. Flipping the hand moves it to the other jamb and leaves the swing side alone. A door with no arc in any plan, or two arcs a jamb apart (a pair of leaves), is named rather than guessed. - **The To Room.** This is what door schedules and door numbers read. Revit sets it at placement, and a facing flip does NOT move it: four doors flipped to swing toward their offices still read "To Corridor". So it is checked on its own, and swapped with Revit's From/To flip when wrong. A door still wrong on any count is named rather than counted. **EVERY DOOR IS READ BACK.** Its host must be the wall that was found. One that Revit hosted somewhere else, or nowhere, is removed again inside the same undo and its point named. **NOTHING IN THIS LIBRARY COULD PUT A DOOR IN A WALL.** Measured 2026-09-18: every `NewFamilyInstance` call in the 372 fragments passes a point, a face or a view, and not one passes a HOST ELEMENT. So the most ordinary architectural act there is had no route at all. **A DOOR PLACED WITHOUT ITS HOST IS NOT A DOOR.** Revit will place some families free-standing and they then cut nothing, schedule wrong, and do not move when the wall moves. That is why the wall is found and the door read back, rather than the host being left to a name: the failure is silent and looks fine in plan. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **symbol** - by name, as Revit writes it<br>**points** - points - MILLIMETRES, "x,y,z"; several separated by semicolons - "0,0,0; 5000,0,0"<br>**to room at** - points - MILLIMETRES, "x,y,z"; several separated by semicolons - "0,0,0; 5000,0,0"<br>**hinge at** - points - MILLIMETRES, "x,y,z"; several separated by semicolons - "0,0,0; 5000,0,0"<br>**level** - a level, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused<br>**sill height** - text<br>**rotation** - text |
| **You get** | placed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `PLACE_HOSTED_FAMILY` |

Once it is proved, you will ask: *"put a door in this wall"* · *"place windows in this wall"* · *"add a door here"*

<a id="place-line-based-family"></a>

### Place line based family

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put a beam or a brace along each of these lines.

Places a line-based family along each curve given - a beam, a brace, anything whose family is driven by a LINE rather than by a point. **EVERY OTHER PLACEMENT IN THIS LIBRARY IS POINT-BASED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON THIS EXISTS.** `PLACE_FAMILY_INSTANCES` takes `IList<XYZ>`, which is right for diffusers, sprinklers and detectors and cannot express a beam at all: a beam has a start and an end, and the family is driven by the line between them. Measured 2026-09-18 against the whole library - not one fragment called the curve overload, so braces and every curve-driven loadable family were unreachable. **THE STRUCTURAL TYPE IS ASKED FOR AND NEVER ASSUMED.** A beam and a brace are the same call with a different `StructuralType`, and Revit's analytical behaviour, the schedules and the load take-off all follow it. Guessing it is how a brace lands in the model as a beam and nothing says so. **THE SYMBOL IS ACTIVATED FIRST.** An unactivated type places nothing and reports no error - the same trap `PLACE_FAMILY_INSTANCES` exists to close. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a run of twelve beams is one undo entry rather than twelve.

Every one is a straight line; an arc cannot be written<br>**level** - a level, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused<br>**structural type** - text |
| **You get** | placed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |

<a id="place-model-groups"></a>

### Place model groups

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** place new instances of this model group type at these points.

Places an instance of an existing model group type - the typical toilet block, the repeated plant arrangement - once at each point given, on a level. GROUP_ELEMENTS makes a group from elements; until this fragment nothing could place another instance of one. **THE GROUP TYPE IS NAMED** - as the Project Browser shows it under Groups > Model. A name that matches no model group type is refused with the ones that exist; a DETAIL group is refused, because it belongs to a view and is placed differently. **EACH POINT IS X AND Y ON THE PLAN, AND Z ABOVE THE LEVEL**, in millimetres - the group's origin goes there. Each instance's level and offset are read back from Revit after placing, never assumed. **EACH ONE PLACED IS A GROUP, AND EVERY GROUP RULE COMES WITH IT.** Its members refuse to move one by one and are changed for every instance at once - GROUP_ELEMENTS's card says why that matters. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16). One operation is one undo entry, and the caller owns it.

<a id="remap-line-styles"></a>

### Remap line styles

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** move every line off one line style and onto another.

Moves every line in the model off one line style and onto another - the cleanup after an imported drawing, after inheriting somebody else's template, or after the office standard was renamed. It is also the step that has to happen before the old style will purge. **THE REASON A STYLE STILL WILL NOT PURGE AFTER SOMEBODY "MOVED EVERYTHING": LINES LIVE IN PLACES A SELECTION CANNOT REACH.** Model and detail lines placed in views are the ones a rubber band finds. Lines inside SKETCHES - a floor's boundary, a ceiling's edge, a stair riser - are curve elements owned by a sketch, selectable in no view, and are the usual reason. Both are walked here, and counted separately so the difference is visible. **FILLED REGION BORDERS ARE THE THIRD PLACE, AND REVIT WILL NOT TELL US WHICH ONES USE THE OLD STYLE.** There is a setter for a region's border style and no getter, on every release here. So there is no honest way to change only the offending regions, and `filledRegionMode` says so instead of pretending: count them, set them ALL, or leave them. Setting all is blunt and is the only route that actually lets the old style purge. **A LINE INSIDE A LOADED FAMILY CANNOT BE REACHED FROM THIS DOCUMENT AT ALL.** It belongs to the family, not the project. Nothing here can move it, so nothing here pretends to - if the style still refuses to purge with every count at zero, that is where it is, and the report says so. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | moved, placed found, sketch found, regions set |

<a id="replace-material"></a>

### Replace material

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** swap this material for that one everywhere these elements use it.

Swaps one material for another everywhere the elements handed in use it - inside the layers of walls, floors and roofs, and on the material parameters of instances and their types. The "this finish was wrong" or "the client changed the spec" job, without opening every type dialog by hand. **A material hides in more than one place, and a swap that misses one leaves the old material half in use** - which then refuses to purge, and nobody can see why. Two places are covered here: the LAYERS of a type's compound structure, and every material-valued PARAMETER on an instance or its type. **"<By Category>" is not "no material".** It is an invalid element id, and reading it as empty is how a swap quietly misses everything that was set by category. That trap is why this reports what it examined and not only what it changed. **Editing a type changes every element of that type, not just the ones selected.** Two walls of one type are ONE type: change it through either and both change. That is Revit working correctly and it still surprises people, so types touched are counted separately from elements handed in. **An element inside a group is left alone for instance parameters.** Unless the parameter is flagged as varying across groups, the write is either refused or - worse - applied to every instance of that group in the model. Neither announces itself, so grouped elements are skipped and the count is reported rather than hidden. Layers are unaffected: they live on the type, which a group does not own. **Three type families are skipped by name** - curtain walls, sloped glazing and basic ceilings. They report a compound structure that is not a real layer stack, and writing to it misbehaves. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). There is no dry-run switch: previewing is the host's approval gate.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **find material** - a value<br>**replace material** - a value |
| **You get** | layers changed, parameters changed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `REPLACE_MATERIAL` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.

Other ways to ask: *"why will this material not purge"* · *"swap this material for that one"*

<a id="report-joined-elements"></a>

### Report joined elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what is this joined to, and which one is cutting which.

Reports, for each element handed in, what Revit has joined it to and which side of each join is doing the cutting. **A join is invisible until it is wrong.** Nothing on screen says two elements are joined; what shows is a wall that stops short, a beam that has lost its end, or a takeoff that is quietly short by the overlap. This is the read that turns "the quantities look wrong" into a list. **Which one CUTS is the half nobody remembers to ask.** A join always has a direction: one element gives its overlap to the other. Two walls joined the wrong way round look almost identical in plan and produce different volumes, different material takeoffs and a different section. So the direction is reported for every pair, not just the fact of the join. **It reports and changes nothing.** JOIN_GEOMETRY separates a pair or turns one round; both are hard to undo across a model, and the honest first step is to look. **An element joined to nothing is a normal answer.** Most elements are, and an empty list against a wall is not a failed read - the count of elements with no joins at all is reported so the two cannot be confused.

| **You get** | joins, findings |

<a id="report-roof-reach"></a>

### Report roof reach

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** is there a gap between two roofs: how far the end of one roof stops short of the other roof's upper face, measured with rays - a read.

Says whether one roof reaches another, as a read only. Two roofs are selected; rays are cast from each end of each roof - a roof by extrusion's two ends, a roof by footprint's gable ends - toward the other roof alone, in the 3D view given, and only a hit on the other roof's upper face counts. The answer is yes when an end meets that face or the two roofs overlap, and no with the gap in millimetres - the nearest and farthest point of the end - when it stops short. No end facing the other roof is said as that, never as the roofs being apart. The other roof must show in the 3D view.

Answers a question, and changes nothing in the model: which walls are held by a roof through Attach Top/Base. Each wall that is held is named, with its type, which end is held - its top, its base, or both - and the roof that holds it, by name and id. The roofs in the selection are the ones the question is about, and any roof counts when none is selected; the walls in the selection are the ones read, and every wall in the model is read when none is selected. Anything else in the selection is named and left out. A wall that could not be read is named with the reason and is never counted as free. Revit 2020 to 2024 record only whether a wall end is held, not by what - it may be a floor or a ceiling as well as a roof - so on those releases the answer lists those walls apart and says plainly that the roof cannot be confirmed. Revit 2025 and later name the element itself.

**What it does:** change one layer of a wall or floor type - its thickness, material or function.

Changes one layer in a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's build-up - its thickness, its material, its function, any of the three - and reports what it was before. Or reads the layer, or checks it against values, and changes nothing. **A LAYER'S MATERIAL IS TYPE DATA, AND IT HAD NO ROUTE.** Version 1 set the width alone, so a wall's colours went on by painting faces - which is not the type, and schedules as nothing. The material is given by its name and must already be in the project; a name that is not refuses the call, naming the closest that are. `CREATE_STARTER_MATERIALS` makes one by name. `<By Category>` clears it. **BLANK MEANS LEAVE IT.** `material` and `layerFunction` blank and `widthMm` 0 read the layer as it stands; `checkOnly` compares what is given and writes nothing. **`REPORT_COMPOUND_STRUCTURE` READS THE BUILD-UP AND NOTHING WROTE IT.** So *"modify thickness"* - asked plainly, and the ordinary answer to a spec change - had no route. `WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` cannot reach a layer: a wall's thickness is not an instance parameter, it is the sum of its layers. **IT IS A TYPE CHANGE AND IT REACHES EVERY INSTANCE.** This is the thing to say before running it, not after. Editing the build-up of *Basic Wall: 200 Blockwork* changes every one of them in the model. If that is not wanted, `DUPLICATE_TYPE` first and edit the copy - and the finding says so in every run. **THE STRUCTURE IS READ, CHANGED AND WRITTEN BACK AS A WHOLE.** Revit hands out a COPY of the compound structure, so changing it in place does nothing at all until it is set back on the type. That silent no-op is the mistake this fragment exists to make impossible. **THE LAYER IS BY INDEX, AND THE INDEX IS REVIT'S** - 0 is the outside face. `-1` finds it by its function instead, and two layers with that function are refused by number rather than one guessed at. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | applied, was mm, build up, matches, differences, findings |
